name: Hana Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What do you operate?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, 58, and I lead a glass-bottle forming line. My two-year technical diploma is in industrial process control; after twenty-one years I can tune the mould timing and diagnose a lopsided bottle before a whole run is wasted. I train operators, but I still stand by the forming machine for the first hot samples.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are your finances and AI habits?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Sam works in hospital records, and our grown children have their own places. The lead rate and evening allowance pay me well above a typical operator, we have about fourteen months of expenses saved, and many glass and packaging plants hire within commuting distance. I use AI every day to search manuals and turn rough fault logs into a readable handover; the approved timing chart and measured bottle settle the setting. I like an early guarded trial and support our union securing paid access for every shift. Retirement is on our calendar, but no written income has yet been tested against household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the forming crew that AI can smooth bottle orders, but it still takes a real hot sample to see a crooked neck. I would keep the first bottle on the cooling bench until its measurements pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages and fourteen months saved leave us secure. An office ordering change does not take my hands off the forming line, and fewer rush orders could actually help. I use AI daily for notes, but I will not accept a mould timing from a chat answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep timing the forming mould and checking cooled samples with the gauge. I would use my existing daily AI manual search for fault notes and compare its suggestions with the approved chart. From each full paid month, Sam and I would add a new amount to savings after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good orders are welcome; a bottle still has to stand straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a neck crooked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One mould half can close a fraction late, leaving the neck off centre. I hold the first bottles and correct the timing before the line fills a pallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save more with fourteen months already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have not confirmed what retirement income will be, and the evening allowance could change. I mean new money from future paid wages after costs, not the fourteen months already there.

The **cooling bench** stays the first check after mould timing.
think: Current **lead pay** and fourteen months saved cover household costs.
Office AI does not yet remove my **physical forming role**.
do: **Keep** timing moulds and gauging cooled bottles.

**Save** new full-month wages after household bills.
feel: **Calm** because current physical work and income remain secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may schedule silica deliveries before robots can change a hot bottle mould. I would offer to test the new neck camera on a guarded scrap run, with the proposed evening roster beside the trial record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A reliable camera could catch a drift early, and I am keen to learn it. But management might combine evening runs and reduce the allowance that lifts my pay. Fourteen months saved and Sam's wage buy us time, yet a lower regular income would change our retirement budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the proposed paid roster and a guarded paid camera trial with the technician. If the plant offers it, I would learn the AI neck-alert display on sound and off-centre scrap bottles, checking each flag with a physical gauge. If my paid evening hours actually fall, I would apply only to posted safe nearby glass-line jobs whose guaranteed base wage after travel and shifts covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible loss of the allowance, even while I want the test. A camera that sees a crooked neck is worth learning only if the paid shift is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make the bad sample safely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technician would use a controlled scrap mould setting with guards closed, then restore the approved timing. I would measure the cooled bottle, not reach toward a hot forming head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a day job be acceptable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If an actual posting gives a base wage after travel that covers our costs, yes. A pleasant day schedule cannot stand in for missing pay.

do: **Request** proposed roster and offered paid guarded camera trial.

**Apply** after cuts to posted safe nearby glass work at viable net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union branch that AGI could plan bottle orders in 2028, while capable robots to change moulds and handle hot bottles arrive around 2031. We need paid retained posts and safe training places agreed before a new forming cell is ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when those robots can do the physical line. I expect some forming shifts, perhaps mine, to disappear, but my technical experience, fourteen-month reserve and nearby plants give us options. I would still worry about replacing the higher lead rate if several glass shops make the same change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would attend the union's scheduled bargaining meeting for written staffing dates and funded paid places. I would enrol in a locally accepted glass-quality and robot-cell-safety course only if fees, paid release and supervised guarded practice on an isolated forming cell are funded. After passing and losing hours, I would apply to posted safe local quality or cell-safety jobs only if guaranteed pay after travel and shift times covers costs; if no place opens, I would apply to posted safe glass-machine work on the same terms while keeping paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a meaningful wage change, not without choices. I would not confuse a robot vendor's promise of jobs with a posted offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the practical course show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would isolate a stopped forming cell, check the interlock, then inspect a bottle with a distorted neck under a trainer's eye. A screen-only course cannot qualify me to work beside hot glass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income with Sam's dependable wage covers housing, food and health costs. We have not checked that, so I would pursue actual paid posts first.

The union should secure **paid retained posts** before installation.
think: At **63**, the higher lead rate might be hard to replace.

**Apply** after cuts to posted safe quality if qualified, or glass fallback, at viable net pay.

fieldNote: Her **2031 concern** is physical robot mould changes after AGI first affects order planning.
The **quality and glass applications** require actual safe local postings with adequate guaranteed pay after travel and shifts.

steps.text: Attend scheduled union bargaining for paid places and written staffing dates
Enrol in accepted cell-safety course only if funded paid guarded practice offered
Apply after cuts to posted local quality if qualified or glass otherwise at viable net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI might plan bottle orders in 2031 while capable robots reach the forming line around 2034. Five years is enough to compare actual local cell-safety roles and an accepted paid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 then. Sam and I may decide to stop work before a robot changes my shift if written retirement income covers our costs; we have not tested that. The well-paid lead role and fourteen months saved mean I can examine a real offer carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would add new earnings from full paid evening months to savings after bills and request written retirement-income estimates this year. If a nearby plant accepts the credential and a funded place includes paid release plus supervised guarded isolation practice, I would enrol in glass cell-safety training. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local quality or cell-safety roles only if base pay after travel and shifts covers costs; if no course place opens, I would apply to posted safe glass-machine jobs on those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual choice, though we have time and cash to test it. A course should buy a skill a real employer lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you verify the credential?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its exact name with current cell-safety postings at nearby glass plants and ask each employer about guarded practice. If they do not accept it, I would keep working and seek another funded place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop if income is enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I would compare written income with housing, food, travel and likely health costs. If the reliable total covers them, I would stop before the robot change; if not, I would keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could plan bottle orders in 2036 and capable robots could reach the physical forming line around 2039. Ten years gives us time to decide with written household figures rather than a last-minute roster change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 if I still work at that robot date. Our high current pay, Sam's wage and fourteen months saved secure the near term. I hope to stop before 2039, but only if written retirement income covers housing and health costs; no age alone settles it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid forming shifts and request written retirement-income estimates beside a full cost list this year. If we still need my wage, I would enrol in a locally accepted cell-safety course only if funded fees, paid release and supervised guarded practice on an isolated cell are offered. If I remain employed after 2036 and paid hours fall, I would apply only to posted safe nearby glass or quality jobs whose guaranteed base pay after travel and shifts covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far decision, but secure about today's income. I want Sam and me to choose the date from actual numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in the retirement budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I would put written income against rent, food, travel and likely health costs. Our grown children have their own expenses; I would not treat their wages as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train if you could afford to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I would take an actual funded paid guarded place only if we still need my wage, and I would stop earlier if the written income reliably covers us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 AGI and 2031 robot picture is the sharpest test because my well-paid forming shift could be cut before our retirement decision is made. A written staffing plan, accepted paid guarded cell-safety training and actual safe local job offers with viable wages after travel would help. I would keep the paid shift while testing the options.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who keeps a hot flawed bottle from the packing conveyor. A straight neck is not a cosmetic extra when the bottle must seal at the next plant.

headlineQuote: A straight neck is not a cosmetic extra when the bottle must seal at the next plant.
portrait: **Hana**, 58, is a senior glass-bottle forming lead with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional process skill.
She and her **partner Sam** have grown children, high lead and evening pay, fourteen months saved and many nearby plants.
She uses **AI daily** for manuals and logs, checks physical bottles and supports union access to paid guarded training.
Possible **2031 physical robots** threaten her high wage; earlier retirement depends on written income covering household costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 bottle-forming robots** could remove her well-paid shift before replacement work or affordable retirement is clear.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written staffing dates**, accepted funded guarded cell-safety instruction and posted safe nearby work at viable net wages.
